title: The loaded generator: synchronous reactance and the phasor

interactive.brief: The one thing you should see is E, the voltage inside, growing on a lagging load and shrinking on a leading one, while the AVR holds V, when you step the power factor.
interactive.title: The phasor drop
interactive.whatAmILookingAt:
Fourteen small screens on one picture, with Back and Continue. Five show an idea and nine ask you to try it. No marks and no timers.

The picture. At the top is one phase of the set, drawn as a small circuit. On the left, a circle marked E is the voltage the set makes inside. Next comes a coil marked Xs, the synchronous reactance. On the right are the terminals, marked V, with the load beyond. A small AVR box measures V and drives a field-current bar beside E, from 0% up. Below it sits the phasor drawing. V lies flat from the origin, 1.0 per unit long. The current arrow I is dashed. It starts at the origin. Its length is the load current. Its angle is the power factor. It points below V when lagging and above V when leading. The drop across Xs is an arrow drawn from V's tip. It stands at right angles to I, 90° ahead of it. E runs from the origin to the drop's tip and closes the triangle. The angle δ is marked between E and V. Two dashed guides split the drop into its part along V and its part across V. Each is labelled with its length. They fade in as the drop leans over, and fade out as the AVR goes off. Each screen keeps one scale, set by the largest triangle it can reach. So V keeps its length while E grows or shrinks. The load slider runs from 0 to 1.0 per unit of rated current, in steps of 0.1. It opens at 1.0. The power factor stepper has five settings, in this order: Zero pf leading, 0.8 leading, Unity, 0.8 lagging and Zero pf lagging. It opens on Unity. The Xs slider runs from 0.1 to 2.0 per unit, in steps of 0.1. It opens at 1.5. An AVR switch turns the AVR on and off.

Four readout tiles show E in per unit, Field current in %, V in per unit and δ in degrees. On a phone they wrap onto two rows. The stepper's five settings and the switch wrap too, so no word splits.

The rule it computes. Everything is one phase, in per unit. 1.0 means the set's rated voltage, 440 V between lines at the terminals, or its rated current. Per unit reads the same on phase and line bases. Per unit is per cent ÷ 100. The winding's resistance is left out. The drop is Xs × I, and it runs 90° ahead of the current, as across any reactance. Split the current in two. Its part in step with V is I × the power factor. Its part at right angles is I × the sine of its angle. That sine is 0.6 at 0.8, 1 at zero power factor and 0 at unity. The in-step part makes a drop across V: Xs × I × the power factor. The other part makes a drop along V: Xs × I × the sine. It is added for a lagging load and taken off for a leading one. With the AVR on, V is held at 1.0. So E's part along V is 1.0 plus or minus that drop. Its part across V is the across drop. E = √(along² + across²). δ is the angle whose tangent is across ÷ along. The field bar is drawn in proportion to E. 100% is the field that makes 1.0 with nothing connected. That is the straight part of the open-circuit curve, carried on. The field current cannot go below zero, because the diodes on the shaft pass current one way only. Only Zero pf leading can ask for less: there E = 1.0 − Xs × I. Past that point the bar sits at 0% in red. E is zero, and V climbs to Xs × I. With the AVR off, the field freezes at exactly the value it had. E keeps the length that field gives. So from unity at rated current it holds 180%, and E holds 1.80. V moves instead: V = √(E² − across²) − Xs × I × the sine, with the same signs. The caption under the picture says that real iron saturates, so a real V never climbs as high as drawn.

Screen 1, try it, a recall. No picture. "A transformer has an R% of 1.5 and an X% of 3. At full load, 0.8 lagging, its output sags 3.0%. At 0.8 leading, the same current lifts its output by 0.6%. Why the difference?" Three choices, in this order: "The leading load draws less current"; "The leading load meets less resistance"; "The angle turns the same drops along or against the output". Right, the third. Each wrong choice has its own hint. Why: the working, step by step. A right Check says "Still there." Read: the question.

Screen 2, show. The AVR on, Unity, Xs at 1.5, the load at 0 and its slider free. At no load, the rated-current triangle is drawn faintly, dashed, and fades as the load rises. The words: "Each phase works like this small circuit. The field makes a voltage inside, E. 100% field makes 1.0 per unit with nothing connected. On its way out, the current passes through a reactance, Xs. The stator's current makes a field of its own, which alters the rotor's. Some flux also leaks past. Both make a voltage that grows with the current and runs 90° ahead of it. Together they act like one reactance, the synchronous reactance.[^1] With no load, V equals E. Drag the load up and watch E grow past V." Read: the words without the controls. Still: the load at 1.0, Unity, the triangle drawn and the readouts at 1.80, 180%, 1.00 and 56°.

Screen 3, try it, typed. The load at 1.0, Unity, the drop arrow hidden until Check. "This set's Xs is 1.5 per unit. Per unit is a fraction of the set's own rating. So 1.0 means 440 V between lines, or rated current. Rated current flows. How big is the drop across Xs, as a line voltage?" A field in V. Answer 660 V. Slips, each with a hint naming the mistake: 6.6 V, 293 V and 381 V. Hint when wrong: "Find the drop in per unit, then multiply by 440 V." Why: the working, step by step. A right Check draws the drop arrow, labelled 1.5. Read: the question.

Screen 4, show. The AVR on, Unity, the load at 1.0, the Xs slider free from 1.5. The words: "The drop across a reactance runs 90° ahead of its current. At unity the current lies along V. So the drop stands straight up from V's tip. E closes the triangle: √(1.0² + 1.5²) = 1.80. The field must make 1.80 to hold 1.0 at the terminals. The angle between E and V is the load angle, δ. Here it is 56°. Drag Xs down to 0.1. That is nearer a transformer's size. E is then barely longer than V." Read: the words without the controls. Still: Xs at 1.5, the load at 1.0, Unity, the right angle and δ marked.

Screen 5, try it, typed. The AVR on, Unity, Xs at 1.5, the E tile reading ? until Check. "At unity, the load falls to half rated current, 0.5 per unit. Xs is 1.5 and the AVR holds V at 1.0. How big must E be?" A field in per unit. Answer 1.25 per unit. Slips, each with a hint naming the mistake: 1.75, 0.25 and 1.80. Hint when wrong: "Find the drop, then use Pythagoras with V." Why: the working, step by step. A right Check slides the load to 0.5. Read: the question.

Screen 6, try it, a prediction. The AVR on, the load at 1.0, Xs at 1.5, Unity. The E, Field current and δ tiles read ? throughout. "Predict before you look. Two loads draw rated current from the set. One is at 0.8 lagging and one is at 0.8 leading. The AVR holds V at 1.0. Which needs more field current?" Three choices, in this order: "Neither, the current is the same"; "The 0.8 lagging load"; "The 0.8 leading load". Right, the second. Each wrong choice has its own hint. Why: the working, step by step. A right Check steps to 0.8 leading, then to 0.8 lagging, and the field bar climbs. Read: the question.

Screen 7, show. The AVR on, the load at 1.0, Xs at 1.5, the stepper free from Unity. No readout tiles on this screen; the field bar shows the field. The words: "Step the power factor to 0.8 lagging. The current swings 37° behind V. The drop swings round with it. Now it leans forward along V. Split the current in two. Its 0.8 in step with V makes a drop across V, 1.5 × 0.8 = 1.2. Its 0.6 lagging part makes a drop along V, 1.5 × 0.6 = 0.9. So E's part along V grows to 1.9. Watch the field bar climb." Read: the words without the controls. Still: 0.8 lagging, the load at 1.0, the guides labelled 1.2 and 0.9. The 1.2 sits low on its guide, below where E crosses it.

Screen 8, try it, typed. The AVR on, 0.8 lagging, the load at 1.0, the E and Field current tiles reading ? until Check. "Rated current flows at 0.8 lagging. Xs is 1.5 and the AVR holds V at 1.0. How big must E be?" A field in per unit. Answer 2.25 per unit. Slips, each with a hint naming the mistake: 1.80, 2.50 and 1.20. Hint when wrong: "Add the along parts, then use Pythagoras with the across part." Why: the working, step by step. A right Check shows the field bar at 225%. Read: the question.

Screen 9, show. The AVR on, the load at 1.0, Xs at 1.5, the stepper free from 0.8 lagging, the load slider free. The words: "Step to 0.8 leading. The current swings ahead of V, so the drop leans back. E's part along V falls to 1.0 − 0.9 = 0.1, so E falls to 1.20. Step on to Zero pf leading, the current capacitors alone draw. The whole drop now points back against V. Drag the load up. Partway, the field bar hits zero and turns red. The diodes on the shaft pass current one way only, so the field cannot reverse. V climbs above 1.0." Read: the words without the controls. Still: Zero pf leading, the load at 1.0, the field bar at 0% in red, E at 0 and V at 1.50.

Screen 10, try it, typed. The AVR on, Zero pf leading, the load at 0, the Field current tile reading ? until Check. "A set feeds only correction capacitors, left in after the rest of the load has gone. That is a Zero pf leading load. Xs is 1.5 and the AVR holds V at 1.0. At what current does the field reach zero?" A field in per unit. Answer 0.67 per unit. Slips, each with a hint naming the mistake: 1.5 and 1.0. Hint when wrong: "The drop points straight back against V. E is zero when the drop equals V." Why: the working, step by step. A right Check slides the load up until the field bar turns red. Read: the question.

Screen 11, show. The load at 1.0, Xs at 1.5, Unity, the AVR on. The AVR switch is free, and the stepper offers only 0.8 leading, Unity and 0.8 lagging. The words: "Hold rated current at unity with the AVR on. E is 1.80 and the field 180%. Now switch the AVR off. The field stays at 180%, so E keeps its length. Step to 0.8 lagging. E's tip swings round a circle, and V shrinks to close the triangle. Step to 0.8 leading, and V grows. This is why the voltage sagged on load with the AVR off." Switching the AVR off at unity leaves V at 1.00. Read: the words without the controls. Still: the AVR off, the load at 1.0, 0.8 leading, E at 1.80, the field at 180% and V at 2.25.

Screen 12, try it, typed. The AVR off, the field at 180%, the load at 1.0, Unity, the V tile reading ? until Check. "With the AVR on at unity and rated current, the field sat at 180% and E at 1.80. The AVR is now off. The same current swings to 0.8 lagging. E's part across V is 1.2 and the drop's part along V is 0.9. What is V now?" A field in per unit. Answer 0.44 per unit. Slips, each with a hint naming the mistake: 0.90, 0.30 and 1.00. Hint when wrong: "E's part along V is √(1.80² − 1.2²). Take 0.9 off that." Why: the working, step by step. A right Check steps to 0.8 lagging and shrinks V. Read: the question.

Screen 13, try it, typed (mixed). The AVR on, the load at 1.0, Xs at 1.5, 0.8 lagging, the δ tile reading ? until Check. "Rated current flows at 0.8 lagging. Xs is 1.5 and the AVR holds V at 1.0. What is the load angle δ between E and V?" A field in degrees. Answer 32 degrees. Slips, each with a hint naming the mistake: 37 and 58. Hint when wrong: "Find E's parts along and across V. tan δ = across ÷ along." Why: the working, step by step. A right Check marks δ. Read: the question.

Screen 14, try it, typed (mixed). The AVR on, the load at 1.0, Xs at 1.5, 0.8 lagging, the readouts showing. "Sets are rated at 0.8 power factor. So the winding and the field are built for rated current at 0.8 lagging, as drawn here. A 630 kVA set runs at 440 V between lines. What line current flows at its full rating?" A field in A. Answer 826.7 A. Slips, each with a hint naming the mistake: 1431.8, 661.3 and 477.3. Hint when wrong: "Line current = VA ÷ (√3 × the line voltage)." Why: the working, step by step. A right Check shows the closing line: "A lagging load needs more field, a leading one less." Read: the question.
interactive.ignores: The picture shows one phase, in per unit. The winding's resistance is left out. A real winding adds a small drop in step with the current. The field bar is drawn in proportion to E. That carries on the straight part of the open-circuit curve. Real iron saturates, so a large E costs more field than drawn. For the same reason, V cannot climb as far as drawn with the AVR off on a leading load. Xs is one fixed example value. In a real machine it changes with saturation. On a salient-pole rotor it differs along and across the poles. These are steady values. In the first moments after a sudden change, a smaller reactance acts. The floor is drawn at zero field current. A real set can lose control of its voltage before its field reaches zero. The speed is held steady, so the frequency never moves. The AVR settles at once.

explain.text:
A loaded generator drops voltage inside itself, as a transformer does. In each phase the field makes a voltage inside, E. The load current pushes through a reactance on its way to the terminals. So E must be the terminal voltage V plus that drop. They add as arrows, tip to tail.

Two effects make that reactance. The stator's current makes a field of its own. That field alters the rotor's. Some of the winding's flux also leaks past. Both make a voltage that grows with the load current and runs 90° ahead of it. That is just how a reactance behaves. So together they act like one reactance in series with each phase. This is the [[synchronous reactance]], Xs.[^1] The winding has resistance too. It is small, so it is left out here. Xs is given as a fraction of the set's own rating, in [[per unit]]. Per unit is per cent ÷ 100. So it is your percentage impedance in another form. Here Xs is 1.5 per unit, an example value. So rated current drops 1.5 times the terminal voltage inside. That is 150%, against an X% of 3 for the transformer at the start.

The drop across a reactance runs 90° ahead of its current. At unity power factor the current lies along V. So the drop stands at right angles from V's tip. With V held at 1.0 and rated current flowing, E = √(1.0² + 1.5²) = 1.80. Now let the same current lag at 0.8. Its 0.8 in step with V makes a drop across V, 1.5 × 0.8 = 1.2. Its 0.6 lagging part makes a drop along V, 1.5 × 0.6 = 0.9. So E = √(1.9² + 1.2²) = 2.25. At 0.8 leading, that 0.9 points back against V. Then E = √(0.1² + 1.2²) = 1.20. The angle between E and V is the [[load angle]], δ. It is 56° at unity and 32° at 0.8 lagging.

The field makes E. So with the AVR on, a lagging load needs more field current to hold the same terminal voltage. Here 100% field is the field that makes 1.0 with nothing connected. At the same current, a leading load needs less. A big enough load of capacitors alone would need less than none. The field cannot give that, because the diodes on the shaft pass current one way only. With the AVR off, the field holds E's length, so V moves instead. At the same current, V is lower on a lagging load than at unity, and higher on a leading one. These figures come from a simplified picture. It puts the field in proportion to E and leaves out resistance. Real iron saturates, so a lagging load costs more field still. **For the same terminal voltage and current, a lagging load needs a larger voltage inside the machine than a leading load does.**

Leading loads turn up on the job. Correction capacitors left in on a light load lead. So can a lightly loaded UPS and discharge lighting.[^2] Makers warn that only slightly leading power factor can make a set lose voltage control.[^3] A real set can lose control well before its field reaches zero.

Sets are rated at 0.8 power factor.[^4] So a 630 kVA set gives 630 × 0.8 = 504 kW. At 440 V between lines it carries 630 000 ÷ (√3 × 440) = 826.7 A. Its winding is built for that current, and its field for that current at 0.8 lagging. A load that lags more asks for more field than the set was built to give.

analogy.text: Think of a long run of big cable feeding a motor. To land 440 V at the motor, the board end must sit higher by the cable's drop. For a big cable, your voltage-drop tables give an r part and an x part. A lagging motor tips the x part's drop round towards the voltage, so it counts for more. A generator works the same way. Its cable is inside the machine, and its x is enormous.
analogy.breaks: A cable's drop is a few per cent, so adding its parts straight is close enough. A generator's drop is bigger than its output. So the part at right angles counts too, and you need the whole triangle. Last, the supply fixes a cable's board end, but E moves with the field.

practice.text:
**Working out the voltage inside**

- Put V along the reference at 1.0 per unit.
- Split the load current. The part in step with V is I × the power factor. The part at right angles is I × the sine of its angle.
- Multiply each part by Xs. The in-step part gives the drop across V. The other gives the drop along V. Add it for a lagging load and take it off for a leading one.
- Find E's part along V, 1.0 plus or minus that drop. Then E = √(along² + across²). δ is the angle whose tangent is across ÷ along.
- Multiply by the base, here 440 V, to read E in volts.

**Rules of thumb:** at the same current, the more lagging the load, the more field it takes. A leading load takes less than a unity or lagging one. So capacitors on a lightly loaded set can leave the AVR little room to cut the field.

**Worked example:** a set with Xs of 1.5 per unit carries half its rated current, 0.5 per unit, at 0.6 lagging. The AVR holds V at 1.0. The sine of the current's angle is 0.8. Across V: 1.5 × 0.5 × 0.6 = 0.45. Along V: 1.0 + 1.5 × 0.5 × 0.8 = 1.6. E = √(1.6² + 0.45²) = 1.66 per unit. On the 440 V base, that is 1.66 × 440 = 730 V. δ = tan⁻¹(0.45 ÷ 1.6) = 16°. With the field in proportion to E, it sits at 166% of its no-load value.

**Common mistakes**
- Adding the drop straight onto V. That gives 1.0 + 1.5 = 2.5 at any power factor. Only the part along V adds straight.
- Drawing the drop in line with the current. A reactance's drop runs 90° ahead of it.
- Reading per unit as per cent. 1.5 per unit is 150%, not 1.5%.
- Mixing up δ with the power factor's angle. The power factor's angle lies between I and V. δ lies between E and V.
- Treating a leading load as harmless. The AVR must cut the field for it. Enough of it takes the field to its floor.
